summary:
We developed The Burn Record, an interactive geospatial web application that transforms multi-decade NASA FIRMS active-fire archives into calibrated, easy-to-read fire intelligence for any country or custom polygon.

Raw satellite fire records contain artificial spikes whenever new spacecraft or higher-resolution sensors launch, creating false trends that mask true environmental change. Our platform solves this through an automated harmonization pipeline: it filters out low-confidence detections and static industrial heat sources, normalizes counts by active constellation size across Terra, Aqua, SNPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21, and cross-calibrates 1 km MODIS data to 375 m VIIRS equivalents using overlap-month ratios. Users can evaluate current fire activity against historical baselines through annual anomaly stripes, density and change-vs-baseline maps, timelapses, diurnal solar burn clocks, and downloadable field reports.

This project is important because comparing today's fires against a distorted baseline obscures real climate and land-use shifts. By removing sensor-transition bias, The Burn Record helps researchers, responders, and communities separate genuine wildfire anomalies from satellite artifacts.
details:
We built The Burn Record, an interactive web app that turns multi-decade NASA FIRMS active-fire archives into calibrated historical baselines that anyone can explore. Right now, the live demo comes preloaded with 10 countries so anyone testing it can click straight into working archives, and we are rolling out the rest of the world's countries over the course of the week.

When you look at raw satellite fire records across decades, you see huge artificial spikes whenever new spacecraft launch or higher-resolution sensors take over. Our app fixes that by filtering out low-confidence detections and static industrial heat sources, normalizing counts by how many satellites were active each day across Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21, and scaling older 1 km MODIS data to match 375 m VIIRS using overlap-month ratios. Users can explore annual anomaly stripes, density and change maps, timelapses, and downloadable field reports for any loaded country or custom drawn area. By removing sensor bias, The Burn Record helps researchers and communities separate real wildfire changes from satellite upgrades.

The Burn Record is a web app that takes multi-decade NASA FIRMS active-fire archives and turns them into calibrated historical baselines that anyone can explore. Our current submission is a working demo preloaded with 10 countries ready to click and explore right away, and we are adding the remaining countries across the week since the backend automatically loads any new country archive dropped into its data folder.

When you look at raw satellite fire files over twenty-plus years, you see huge artificial jumps whenever new satellites launch or when higher-resolution sensors take over. To fix that, our app cleans the data in four steps before plotting anything. First, it drops low-confidence detections and optionally filters out non-vegetation heat sources like volcanoes, gas flares, and industrial plants. Next, it divides each detection by how many satellites of that sensor type were active on that day across Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21. Then it compares the overlap period after 2012 between 1 km MODIS and 375 m VIIRS to calculate a scaling ratio (either a single factor or one per calendar month), scales the older MODIS detections up to match VIIRS, and splices the two records together without double-counting. Users can click any highlighted country on the world map, search for a territory, draw their own polygon or circle, or enter coordinates to explore annual comparisons, heatmaps, cumulative burn pacing, timelapses, and downloadable CSV or Markdown reports.

The main benefit is that it stops people from misreading satellite upgrades as real wildfire surges. If you compare raw MODIS numbers from the 2000s directly against modern VIIRS numbers, almost every country looks like it is burning way more than it actually is, so we show both the uncalibrated and harmonized trends side by side. It also removes the need to write custom GIS scripts just to answer basic questions about whether a fire season is running early, late, or unusually high. Our goal is to give researchers, local planners, and everyday users a fast, honest way to check historical fire patterns for a specific country, park, or watershed and export clean data they can actually use.

We built the entire project in Python using Streamlit for the web interface, along with custom CSS and fonts for the layout. On the data side, we used Pandas, NumPy, and PyArrow to parse large CSV files and cache cleaned Parquet copies on disk so repeat loads happen in seconds. For mapping and spatial math, we used GeoPandas, Shapely, Folium, Natural Earth country boundaries, and Esri and OpenStreetMap base tiles, paired with Plotly and Matplotlib for the charts, color scales, and animated timelapses. All of the fire detections come from NASA FIRMS archives covering MODIS and VIIRS.

On the creative side, we borrowed the idea of climate warming stripes and built an annual fire anomaly strip across the top of the app so you can see decades of heavier and quieter fire seasons in a single glance. We also wrote a field notes generator that reads the live numbers for whatever area you select and writes short, plain-English observations about seasonal peaks, single-day extremes, and multi-year streaks. While building it, we had to think carefully about both scientific honesty and performance. For example, we kept Fire Radiative Power separate from the count scaling because intensity is not the same thing as detection count, we added notes explaining that the 24-hour burn clock reflects satellite overpass times rather than when fires actually burn, and we avoided guessing between crop fires and wildfires where the raw data cannot tell them apart. Technically, large countries can have millions of rows, so we used categorical columns, integer grid IDs, and fast array sampling to keep the maps responsive, and we added manual coordinates for thirty small island nations and microstates that are missing from standard low-resolution world maps.
